claim_summary: Proposes a hierarchical multi-agent Agentic RAG in which a ReAct master agent routes each request to a task-specialized sub-agent built on fine-tuned SLMs with retrieval-conditioned prompt pools, evaluated on forecasting, imputation, classification and anomaly detection.

claim_evidence.quote: Our Agentic RAG framework presents a hierarchical, multi-agent architecture composed of a master (top-level) agent and specialized sub-agents customized

modules.name: ReAct master agent routing to sub-agents
modules.scope_reason: R3 tests: TSK no (routing picks a sub-agent but embeds no task output requirement or validator; adding a task adds a tool rather than redesigning the master); GTS no (no temporal semantics at master level); GH yes (delegation and execution control). Counterfactual for TSK: not triggered.
rubric_path: R3_1_TSK:no - routing only, no task objective or validator
R3_2_GTS:no - no temporal semantics at master level

evidence.quote: In summary, the master agent orchestrates sub-agents, selects the most appropriate sub-agent, and allocates the task to the specialized sub-agent.

modules.name: Task-specialized sub-agents
modules.scope_reason: R3_1_TSK yes: each sub-agent's objective, training data and output (forecast, imputation, cluster label, anomaly score) is fixed to one task family. Counterfactual holds: changing the task family requires a different fine-tuned SLM, prompt pool and output procedure.
rubric_path: R3_1_TSK:yes - per-task objective and output; counterfactual holds

evidence.quote: It comprises a master agent that coordinates specialized sub-agents, each dedicated to a specific time series task such as forecasting, anomaly detection, or imputation.
However, in this work, the sub-agents operate in isolation, each handling only a single, specific task.
We evaluated the Agentic-RAG framework using a single, universal sub-agent for all tasks versus specialized subagents for each task.

modules.name: DPO alignment with dynamic masking
modules.scope_reason: R2 LLM: preference optimization updates SLM parameters; the masked binary classification supplies the preference signal. R6: aligns analytical outputs, so instruction_reasoning.

evidence.quote: Additionally, we fine-tune using DPO[8] through a dynamic masking technique to align the SLMs task-specific outputs to preferred and non-preferred outcomes, providing adversarial feedback[47] through a binary classification task.

modules.name: Retrieval-conditioned dynamic prompt pool
modules.scope_reason: R2 LLM: retrieved prompt values are concatenated to the model input embedding and projected by a learnable matrix, changing how the model receives the temporal input; the pool is described as differentiable. A Harness memory reading (GTS context_memory) is possible; see notes.
rubric_path: R2:LLM - alters model input representation with learnable projection

evidence.quote: the prompt pools store both domain and task-specific knowledge as key-value pairs.

data, we utilize a differentiable dynamic prompting mechanism[3].

notes: Blind pass. Role fixed_workflow: the ReAct master can chain sub-agents, but the paper states that here sub-agents operate in isolation on one task each (L117-118), and no evaluated case shows returned feedback changing later actions. Dynamic prompt pool placed in LLM by the R2 test (concatenation into the input embedding, learnable projection, differentiable); low confidence. Excluded as off-the-shelf or protocol: SelfExtend long-context attention from [19] (L325-326, L373); the anomaly threshold (Eq. 1); k-means regime labels for classification; the missing-data simulation. Ablations (Tables 14-18) are evidence, not modules. Process validity and decision utility are not reported.
